title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
raw_text: Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia. Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology. To understand how existing technology environments shape an organization’s ability to operationalize AI, Google Cloud partnered with Hypothesis Group to survey 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The findings reveal a critical paradox: the legacy software systems enterprises rely on to deliver technology to their employees are simultaneously functioning as an innovation tax, actively holding back the AI transformation leaders are trying to achieve. Legacy IT’s operational toll In our study, we defined “legacy” technology as software running locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud. Across industries, decision-makers report that maintaining this footprint exerts a constant friction on their AI ambitions. The consequences to AI are not theoretical. Nearly half (49%) of respondents report that relying on on-premises software has actively delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives. Digging deeper, routine patch application and maintenance emerged as a primary operational bottleneck. As AI-enabled vulnerability discovery accelerates, the rate at which flaws are surfaced in legacy codebases has outpaced what human security teams can realistically address. This creates a zero-sum game between routine maintenance of legacy systems and AI modernization. Instead of directing engineer cycles toward AI modernization, IT teams are spending their time and resources on maintaining legacy systems. Enterprise monoculture Why do organizations continue to rely on legacy environments that constrain their modernization? As our research shows, it is not necessarily architectural preference — but the result of vendor lock-in. Beyond narrowing technology choice, deep provider dependence introduces commercial constraints. In our study, 39% of decision-makers report that reliance on legacy software and cloud providers forces them to navigate complex licensing rules or contracts, or limited negotiating flexibility. Even more concerning is the systemic operational risk created by single-vendor concentration. Concentrating operating systems, productivity applications, cloud hosting and emerging AI models within a single vendor's monoculture creates an immense single point of failure. An autonomous AI agent is only as secure as the operating system and network it traverses. When that underlying stack is vulnerable, organizations are not deploying resilient intelligence; they are expanding their attack surface. Customer choice The solution to vendor lock-in is straightforward: enterprise buyers and policymakers must ensure organizations have genuine choice and interoperability in their software, cloud and AI architectures. Furthermore, 80% of leaders agree that a provider’s installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, while 78% believe that the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. Organizations want the freedom to choose best-of-breed intelligence on its own merits, rather than accepting bundled defaults tied to legacy desktop software. Accelerate agentic technology Delivering this level of autonomous agility across the enterprise requires modern technology built to support the agentic era. Here are a few ideas to get there: Demand architectural and provider choice: AI and cloud must never be held hostage by the legacy software running local servers, email or desktop operating systems. Organizations need the commercial and architectural freedom to select best-of-breed IT on its own merits. Commit to secure-by-design foundations: The industry must move past the broken cycle of releasing insecure software and patching it after the fact. Software manufacturers must engineer durable, resilient architectures where entire vulnerability classes are eliminated before code ever ships — relieving understaffed IT teams from perpetual applying routine but necessary patches. Deploy AI-driven defense to remediate legacy debt: For the millions of lines of vulnerable legacy software already running in production, organizations must shift from manual triage to proactive, AI-assisted defense. By deploying platforms like Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics, teams can use intelligence to continuously surface active exploit paths, prioritize critical exposure and automate remediation across complex, hybrid environments. The promise of agentic AI is to help automate friction away, and accelerate human ingenuity. But that future cannot be built on top of software designed decades ago. As IT leaders plan their roadmaps, it is time to ask: Is your technology foundation accelerating your future, or are you paying a maintenance tax just to keep the past running? Learn more about the research here .
summary: Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia. Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows.

title: Cloud CISO Perspectives: Our security forecast for 2027

This year we’ve witnessed a fundamental change in cybersecurity. When the year began, only a few organizations were using LLMs and agents to find and fix vulnerabilities. Today, it’s happening at scale across enterprises. Organizations expected a reality with agentic hacking where scale, speed and sophistication would outpace human-only response; today, we’re seeing it in practice. Organizations predicted software development at an unheard of pace; today, we’re securing software delivered in hours and days instead of weeks and months. We have passed many milestones, and the world won’t go back — and we are all digging in to fully understand the new reality. The year ahead promises to be challenging, exciting, innovative and will outpace 2026. In the year ahead, enterprise software will change as agility and speed provided by agentic development shifts us from a collection of static applications to a live fabric of autonomous agents that can manage pricing, negotiate supplier contracts, allocate capital, and reroute supply chains in real time. To make this vision a reality, many organizations are rushing to build agents. It’s on us as an industry to ensure the development and operations models are designed to be trustworthy and safe. The risks in 2027 won’t be just server outages or stolen databases. As the agentic operations world takes off, we also need to be concerned about the data and technology foundation that agents rely on. When an agent makes a consequential decision, you must be able to reconstruct the entire story: what inputs came in, how the agent reasoned through them, which tools it called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it. Without that trace, you can't debug it, you can't validate its correctness, and you can't trust it. And if you can't trust it, you can't scale it. Karthik Narain chief product and customer officer, Google Cloud Security must evolve to protect the balance sheet through decision integrity. Every consequential action taken by an autonomous system requires a complete, tamper-proof decision trace, recording and tracking: Inputs entered into the system. How the model reasoned through its decisions. Which tools the model called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it. Collecting this data will help ensure that your teams can reconstruct, validate, and audit every automated decision before scaling. Making the alert queue disappear, from chasing tickets to setting doctrine For decades, security operations centers (SOCs) have suffered from crippling alert fatigue — too many alerts compounded by legacy security tools that hand human analysts half-finished investigations. When autonomous threats can probe a network and move laterally in minutes, human defenders can’t manually stitch together logs across eight different consoles or approve individual defensive actions at microsecond speed. 2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes. Ramya Chitrakar vice-president, Engineering, Google Cloud Security That broken alert queue disappears in 2027 by flipping the operational model. The alert becomes the final output of an investigation. Autonomous defensive agents will handle the data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket. Instead of chasing alerts at a keyboard, human analysts move up the stack to set strategic doctrine, define risk appetite, and verify automated actions built for rapid explainability — where any defensive decision can be understood by a human in 60 seconds and reversed in 30. Moving Beyond Zero: Transaction-level trust and first-class agent identities As enterprises deploy thousands of custom agents across multicloud environments, flat trust architectures, shared human service accounts, and blanket administrator tokens are turning internal workflows into high-leverage entry points for prompt injection and lateral movement. Traditional Zero Trust is too rigid and broad to govern autonomous software acting on its own. We need to extend the Zero Trust concept, not just at the network layer and the machine layer, but now down to the transaction layer. Heather Adkins vice-president, Security Engineering, Google The year ahead demands an architectural shift to Beyond Zero so we can extend verification down to every individual transaction, network packet, and point-in-time authorization. Every autonomous agent should be treated as a first-class identity with its own verifiable credentials, strict least-privileged scope, and open communication standards. When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous. Closing the loop between live runtime and defect-free code The traditional divide between writing software and securing it is breaking down, while adversaries actively target the open-source libraries and external tools that coding assistants pull into codebases. Developers can no longer file a ticket and wait weeks for a manual security review, yet deploying hasty, unvalidated automated patches in production is just as dangerous to business continuity as the vulnerability itself. Adversaries aren't just attacking model math and algorithms. They're actually poisoning the open source software, supply chain, MCP tools, and external libraries that agentic coding assistants pull automatically into code bases. Sandra Joyce vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence In 2027, security becomes a closed-loop, continuous system embedded directly into the software delivery pipeline. By placing agentic reasoning inside developer tools, we can perform threat modeling and catch configuration errors side-by-side as code is written. It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production. Turning internal ground truth into a decisive defender advantage Concerns persist around attackers gaining the upper hand in cybersecurity, and many fear autonomous capabilities will only widen that gap in 2027. Adversaries are already compressing six months of reconnaissance into hours, and exploiting flaws before vendors even know they exist. Compounding the challenge for defenders, no single model can discover or patch every vulnerability across code and cloud on its own. The defender's advantage is that attackers operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork. Defenders own the complete ground truth, identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and real-time runtime activity. Sandra Joyce vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence In the year ahead, defenders will use autonomous technology to capitalize on the one thing an outside attacker will never have: complete internal ground truth. While adversaries operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork, defenders own the full picture of their identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and live runtime activity. By feeding that unified context into multi-model ensembles — such as pairing lightweight models for continuous scanning with deep reasoning models that cross-validate findings and eliminate false positives — organizations can spot and remediate toxic combinations of permissions and configurations that look harmless in isolation, before an external attacker can ever piece them together. Countering asymmetric threat speed and the new extortion playbook Not every adversary will embrace machine speed the same way in 2027. While state-sponsored espionage actors often avoid loud, hyper-fast automated scripts that risk triggering alarms and blowing their long-term stealth, cybercriminals tend to go all-in on autonomous velocity. What we're seeing right now is a variety of adversaries that are exploiting vulnerabilities before the vendors even know about it. Charles Carmakal CTO, Mandiant Consulting As endpoint defenses get better at blocking traditional file-encrypting ransomware, criminal crews are shifting to rapid, high-volume data theft and extortion — specifically targeting proprietary model weights, custom agent skills, prompt libraries, and cloud GPU compute (“ LLMJacking ”). Preparation here means eliminating security silos. It’s a critical failure point to treat models, agent permissions, software supply chains, and cloud infrastructure as separate domains. Instead, we want to unite them under a single, intelligence-led governance framework that allows defenders to lock down high-value autonomous assets and shut down extortion paths before data can leave the environment. Red-teaming the agentic enterprise before adversaries attack In the rush to capture productivity gains in the year ahead, many enterprises are deploying custom agents directly into core business workflows without testing how those systems behave under adversarial pressure. That mistake leaves guardrails vulnerable to bypasses, scanner blinding, and indirect prompt injection. One of the things that the team's been doing over the past few years is doing a lot of red team exercises… with those agentic solutions, so that we have the opportunity to identify and fix the issues before an adversary has the ability to do that against victim organizations. Charles Carmakal CTO, Mandiant Consulting Continuous, proactive adversarial red-teaming must be a mandatory prerequisite before any autonomous workflow touches production. Systematically attempting to break into agentic systems, bypass safety controls, and manipulate model behavior prior to deployment is crucial to securing the agentic era. Critically, model safety engineering should combine the results of those tests with frontline threat intelligence on novel attack prompts and evasion techniques. Defenders can then harden classifiers and neutralize new attack techniques before adversaries can use them against real victims. Orchestrating specialized agent teams to prevent agent sprawl Relying on a single generalist agent to defend an enterprise will fail in 2027 because deep technical skills do not transfer across domains. For example, an agent built to reverse-engineer malware is not the agent that should reason about an identity blast radius. As departments across the business rapidly spin up uncoordinated, standalone agents without centralized oversight, agent sprawl is emerging as the next iteration of shadow IT , threatening to derail enterprise agent deployments through inadequate governance. Technological adoption cannot outpace architectural governance… We have to prioritize machine speed defense. Security cannot remain a manual checkpoint that slows innovation down. Sandra Joyce vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence Just as a well-coordinated human team beats a lone generalist, the year ahead belongs to orchestrated networks of specialized hunter, decoder, and responder agents, each operating with its own domain depth, memory, and dedicated tools. Succeeding at scale requires building the governance and orchestration layer first. The key here will be to establish graduated autonomy, shared state, clean handoffs between specialized agents, and a central coordinator that knows precisely when to act autonomously and when to escalate to a human. To learn more about our cybersecurity guidance for the coming year, check out our Security 2027 video. title: Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
raw_text: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required. Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper . It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it. “The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.” Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post , said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models. Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output. The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios. The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post. The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context. The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt. Microsoft Research said the technique requires no model training. Its researchers described it as an inference-compute attack, meaning a machine with enough memory to run a model has sufficient resources to implant the backdoor. However, the attack requires write access to the model checkpoint. In his research post, Papailiopoulos said a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide the access needed to modify the weights. “What matters is weight, integrity, and provenance,” he added. Modified models can pass evaluations Microsoft researchers said the backdoored models could pass standard evaluations and behave normally until the specified trigger appeared. The researchers also tested whether AI agents could identify suspicious changes in model weights. Their agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4% of held-out modified checkpoints, with a 9.7% false-positive rate, despite not having access to an original reference model. Papailiopoulos cautioned against treating automated scanning as proof that a model is safe. “No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe,” he wrote. According to Papailiopoulos, reliable detection requires comparing a model’s weights with its original, unmodified version. He said establishing a model’s provenance is therefore important to determining whether its weights have been altered between the developer and deployment. Auditing model weights recommended In its accompanying security advisory, Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends auditing model weights before deployment and after every update. Its guidance includes comparing each checkpoint against its declared base model, verifying publishers and file hashes, and rejecting models without verifiable provenance. Microsoft also recommends keeping approved models in private, access-controlled registries rather than allowing agents and inference services to download checkpoints directly from public repositories. For limiting the consequences of a compromised model, Microsoft advises organizations to restrict agent permissions, run agent-generated code in isolated environments, control outbound network connections and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or changing system permissions. Microsoft Research said it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the research’s detection techniques into a red-teaming framework. The company is also exploring AI-assisted weight scanning and cryptographic model signing with verifiable provenance and tamper-evident audit trails. According to the paper, the central idea “was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.”
summary: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required. Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper . It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

title: Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
raw_text: A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian. The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials. “Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post . Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals. Command approvals turn into credential storage Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file. The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it. For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file. Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked. Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens. It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. Passwords embedded in command-line arguments and environment variable assignments often lack the recognizable formats that provider-specific detection rules look for. Leaked credentials on Docker Hub GitGuardian also examined public Docker Hub images and found 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files, 99 of which were valid when detected. The credentials appeared across 543 image repositories and 7625 tags. According to Valadon, the problem arises when developers use Docker’s “COPY..” instruction to copy an entire project working directory into an image. Unlike Git, Docker does not automatically respect the repository’s .gitignore file. Consequently, a Claude Code configuration file excluded from version control can still be copied into a container image unless developers explicitly exclude it through .dockerignore. One valid Cloudflare API token appeared across 559 image tags, while a database password appeared in 643 tags across seven image repositories. Removing the offending file from the GitHub repository does not help the credentials already distributed through published images. Developers must rotate exposed credentials, remove sensitive configuration files from both Git and Docker build contexts, and check previously published images for lingering secrets. GitGuardian recommends treating AI coding assistant configuration files as potential secret-bearing assets, scanning them alongside conventional environment files, and using environment variables rather than hardcoding credentials into commands. Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. GitGuardian said Anthropic’s Claude Code lead Boris Cherny acknowledged the issue, saying the company was looking into it and exploring additional safeguards, including built-in secret scanning and an auto mode.
summary: A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian. The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

title: Why does old access outlive the job?
raw_text: Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews. This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them. Why is granting access easy but removing it hard? Granting has an owner and a deadline. A manager submits a request, an approver clicks yes and the process is completed in just a few hours since someone is involved in it. Removal does not have any of the two. Nobody opens a ticket when permission becomes unnecessary, as the only person who notices will not submit the ticket for lack of reason to do it. The cost of maintaining the permission is high, but it is not visible and it comes in the future. The incentives work the same way. Nobody evaluates how low an access level their team maintains, while a permission that was mistakenly removed and became necessary results in an irate support ticket submitted the same day. And this is something that has to be done via reviews, but, in my opinion, is not done like this. And, at least in all attestation and recertification activities I was involved in, there is simply a basic question for the reviewer: is access still valid? Saying “yes” is not really difficult — access was granted, there were no actions following and reviewing several hundred takes less time than investigating one particular access. This is not what will appear on your screen. When reviewing account names, you do not know whether they were used last week or last year. Role-based access control helps here, but the problem is that, when a user changes his role, his role gets updated, but not the direct access, groups and folders he acquired during the time. What does leftover access actually cost? I have to be quite careful here, as this metric does not reflect the access that remains. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report demonstrated that exploitation of vulnerabilities was the most frequently used method of the breach, making up 31% of all breaches, while the previous leader — abuse of credentials — was reduced to 13%. However, I want to emphasize that this particular report is unrelated to the issue of obsolete permissions. Yet, what the intruder could do after penetrating the system depends on the permissions of the breached account, which in turn depends on the number of permissions acquired. In practice, it looks like findings of audit and investigation, which go on forever, because nobody knows whom exactly to permit to access the corporate data. However, there is information proving the case of the leavers, although quite meager. Thus, according to the PasswordManager.com survey carried out in March 2023, among 1,000 American workers, 58% of the workers who responded that they had used the passwords of their previous employers admitted that they had never updated their passwords after leaving the company. It is an opinion survey carried out online, and that is why it is an indicator. Indeed, I noticed this too: The departures have to go through the HR offboarding checklists, but not the permissions and certificates created by hundreds of people over many years. Transfers are even more of an issue and there are fewer studies regarding them. In the case of a leaver, at least something happens — the offboarding process is triggered. Nothing triggers in case of a transfer. And thus I think that transfers should be equally important as terminations, because the standards require exactly that. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — security and privacy control catalog used throughout organizations — contains AC-2 and AC-6 account management and least privilege controls requiring review of accounts, processing of transfers and terminations, and granting only privileges required by the role of the individual. 3 fixes that make leftover access hard to ignore And here is how I will make sure that the changes will be adopted. There is no need for any new technology to be implemented. Just the decision regarding the ownership of the deletion process. 1. Every change in position will be regarded as an event of deletion Start from the HR record of the system. After the change takes place, generate a task for the outgoing and incoming manager where there will be only one question for the manager to answer — what will the individual no longer need? Provide them with the access list and 10 minutes to answer the question. All the access the individual had created during this period needs to have an owner. If you only do one of these three, do this one. 2. Each permission must have its own unique owner and expiration date Permissions or access to the project folders, special permissions or access to the production system must expire on a particular date, which could be either the date the project expires or, by default, three months after its issuance, unless renewed by the owner, who must be a named person, not an e-mail address. I think of the account, the owner and the applications it accesses as a graph, because if there is any change in accounts, then with one query, it can determine what he/she owns and his/her dependencies. Renewal must be a one-click option, but in the event of that person’s no longer being available, it should be done through his/her manager so that it does not get lost in the cracks. It is a default setting. In the current scenario, if you do nothing, it is your permission; hence, laziness is the dangerous path. Do not make the default action renewing the permission. 3. Present last-used information on all reviews, and allow people to act on it Pull last login and last activity timestamps from your identity provider and application logs and present them along with each entitlement. Order the list such that the least used access appears at the top, select it for removal and ask the reviewer to explain why they need to keep it. From experience, I have found that people are happy to confirm when “this entitlement hasn’t been used in seven months” shows up on the screen. Then allow them to take action based on what they think is best. If attestation takes place using one tool and rotation/vaulting takes place using another tool, then you would find people confirming the question and skipping the action. That’s why I’ve started to keep attestation, rotation, vaulting and retirement of access in one process. Remember, however, there are limitations to this approach. Not all applications maintain usage logs, and sometimes there is legitimate access that is rarely used. Take the case of quarterly close accounts and break glass accounts, for example. They should be assigned an owner and a note. While employees will be able to identify what they don’t need anymore, this is effective only when there is a system in place which allows them to do so safely and easily, and this is yet another reason why we need to implement the three above fixes. In this quarter, start with a single system where sensitive data is stored and run a last-used report on that system. Begin with the users who have been moved to a different role within the past year, since no one has reviewed their access rights since then. Send a list of all those users who haven’t used that system in the past six months to the system owner, and ask them one simple question — Do they still require this? The findings will be enough to make the case for the rest stronger than any framework.
summary: Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access.

title: What will it take to make VulnOps a reality?
raw_text: Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.” VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks. Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea. The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries. As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.” Not your father’s vulnerability management program The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.” Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities. They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices. “The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tells CSO. “We’re now taking that into vulnerability management. If you think about what was different about DevOps, it was the philosophy about going from an iterative cycle to a continuous cycle with fast failure and feedback loops.” Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, argues that AI must become central to how vulnerability management operates. “What we’re talking about here is an AI-centric workflow where the AI is doing most of the analysis, and humans are just overseeing the operation,” Skoudis tells CSO. Not everyone, however, is convinced that VulnOps represents such a fundamental departure from established practices. “It feels like a rebranding to me,” Chris Elgee, SANS principal instructor and senior security analyst at Counter Hack Challenges, tells CSO. “Organizations have always had to deal with vulnerability management,” says Elgee, who agrees that the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery is putting new pressure on organizations, but questions whether VulnOps constitutes a fundamentally different discipline. Is human-in-the-loop dead? Experts disagree on one fundamental aspect of VulnOps as they currently understand the concept. The disagreement centers on how much human control can survive when vulnerability remediation has to operate at AI speed. “The biggest struggle people have with patching vulnerabilities in general is that it’s disruptive to the workflows,” Ali Khan, CISO of AI-powered device security company Iru, tells CSO. “Generally, when there’s a security vulnerability and you need to patch it, you have to upgrade your source code or the third-party supply packages,” Khan explains. “And generally, that leads to breaking changes, especially in legacy systems that have been long-lived and are in maintenance mode,” Khan says. “You don’t want to bring a company down or destroy their revenue stream by pushing a patch that essentially stops the business process.” That risk is why most security professionals aren’t eager to take humans out of the loop. CSA’s Mogull cautions, “We’re nowhere near fully automating [the remediation] part of the process. Eventually, we will need more, but we’re not there yet, even with today’s tools,” he says. Nor does he envision VulnOps operating without human oversight. “Remember, humans are the ones that are accountable,” Mogull says. He points out that under the CSA operating model he helped develop, AI can make decisions within predefined policies, but potentially disruptive changes still require human intervention. SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis argues for what he calls a governance-in-the-loop process where “you have governance that decides that, ‘Hey, if a given action that I take could fall below this governance-in-the-loop level, just do it. Automate it. Don’t even think about it.’” “Each organization is going to have its own separate line for where governance in the loop will apply, but you could say, for example, regarding important patches for Windows workstations, deploy them if they’re critical, on a rolling basis. So, in other words, do 25% per hour or two, over the space of half a day.” Knostic’s Evron, however, believes that even these arrangements may prove unsustainable as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation. “One of the main understandings of the last couple of months is that human in the loop is dead,” he says. “We simply can’t move fast enough for the vast majority of operations to have a human in the loop.” On top of that, Evron questions whether autonomous patching itself will remain an adequate solution. “We must understand that patching is just not going to be fast enough,” Evron says. “We must start considering how we build security programs in a world where patching is not viable.” Autonomous patching may only be transitional Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove inadequate as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation. “Start your program for autonomous patching today, but understand that we need to prepare for a world without patching,” he warns. “If we have a human in the loop, it’s just a performer. The human would have all the responsibility with no authority and no ability to understand and comprehend what they’re doing.” Evron argues that the industry should stop thinking exclusively about finding flaws and fixing them after the fact and should opt instead for software and defensive systems that prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced, detect and neutralize exploitation in the first place, or make individual vulnerabilities less consequential. He sees three approaches to making these preventative systems a reality. The first is to embed them directly into AI coding agents, rather than relying primarily on vulnerability scanning after code has been written. “Control your coding agents and you control your code, so the code itself gets generated more secure,” Evron says. He also advocates scanning code for vulnerabilities upon generation, rather than waiting for it to enter traditional continuous integration pipelines. The second approach is to detect and neutralize attacks at runtime . Evron describes what he calls “patch in place during runtime.” At this year’s [un]prompted conference , Evron went on stage to show ways of conducting patch in place during runtime. “As an attack is going on, it is detected in the logs and patched,” Evron says. The third approach to creating a system that obviates the current patching cycle is to make patching less urgent through defense in depth, according to Evron. He suggests moving toward approaches in which critical vulnerabilities become a matter of defense in depth, “so you don’t necessarily need to patch immediately.” Steps CISOs should be taking now According to Evron, the most critical step CISOs should take in embracing VulnOps is to stop relying solely on established practices that may prevent them from recognizing how AI is fundamentally changing the threat environment. For example, basic security hygiene remains important but cannot be treated as a sufficient response to AI-driven vulnerability discovery, he says. “Stop being afraid to imagine, go bigger, and understand that, well, of course our basics always matter; they will not save us,” he adds. And yet other experts question how organizations can embrace the challenging new world of VulnOps without first nailing down their security basics. Counter Hack’s Elgee says, “A lot of organizations, maybe most organizations, don’t even have a full concept of what their entire asset inventory is.” Iru’s Khan says that CISOs should start to think about how security and engineering need to renegotiate their relationships, given that security teams cannot simply hand developers remediation tickets and expect faster results. “This wall has to come down, and there has to be comfort letting other teams contribute in a technical way to systems,” Khan says. SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis advises CISOs to begin implementing VulnOps without attempting to transform the entire enterprise over to a new paradigm. He argues that organizations should start to establish governance boundaries within which AI agents can operate. “If it’s above the threshold, if it’s higher business risk, then you have to have a human review it,” Skoudis says. “But if it’s below the governance-in-the-loop threshold, push it.” Evron is confident that CISOs can expect their existing teams to handle the transition to VulnOps, particularly if they reduce their dependence on the vulnerability scanning tools that kick out so many vulnerability reports. “The existing teams can handle this, but not with the current technologies they use,” he says. “We must stop paying mindlessly to the big scanning services because the bottleneck has always been fixing and patching.” He adds, “Therefore, building a system where we trust autonomous patching is what we must do right now, in the immediate term, and longer term in our plans we must understand we will not be able to rely on patching.”
summary: Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.” VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks. Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea. The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries.

title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
raw_text: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks. While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies , enterprises should still be concerned. “Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.” Sophisticated tradecraft ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk. The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part. Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained. “This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote. They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual. The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said. The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla. Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode. “ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic. “Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said. This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted. Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory. Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said. A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy. Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said. His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process. But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described. “A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.” ‘A level above’ And, said David Shipley , CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.” Running on premises Exchange has been increasingly risky for years, he noted. For government, AI firms, finance, and other high-value targets, the risk of hosting on prem instead of using cloud-based versions continues to grow. However, it’s worth noting that just having Microsoft host Exchange doesn’t mean you’re safe from nation-states, Shipley said. “It just raises the bar.” Another key challenge with Exchange servers is Microsoft’s own advice not to have anti-virus scanners looking in certain places like ExchangeTransport.exe, because doing so could create instability. “They basically told criminals where to hide and why it’s good to hide there,” he noted. “Not that they can do much about it, but it points to a huge Catch-22.” Another Catch-22: With the publication of this report and new ideas that will undoubtedly come from it, “we’ll likely see criminal groups consider the value of this kind of technique in the future,” Shipley noted.
summary: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

title: One Identity Unveils Active Roles 8.6 with Enhanced Security and Administration

The cumulative release line adds capabilities including the Active Roles REST API, as well as Redistributable Secure Token Server capabilities supporting API access and SAML 2.0 federated authentication. Together with PowerShell and VBScript support, the product keeps familiar tools and interaction patterns at the center of the administrator experience. This combination of configurable views, familiar administration and centralized control supports Active Roles’ position among top Active Directory management solutions . #1 Peerspot Position Strengthens the Ease-of-Administration Story PeerSpot currently ranks Active Roles by One Identity #1 in Active Directory Management , with an 8.5/10 rating based on 92 reviews. It also reports the largest category mindshare at 11.7%, up from 10.4% year over year, and identifies Active Roles as the category’s most popular solution by searches. [peerspot.com] The PeerSpot assessment highlights automated user provisioning, lifecycle management, role-based access control, password resets and streamlined account management among capabilities that reduce manual effort. Feature in focus: Administrator experience with Active Roles 8.6 Active Roles 8.6 is an administrator-experience evolution, combining cumulative security, API and authentication improvements with the product’s established configurable UI, familiar Microsoft-style experience and consolidated hybrid administration. With flexible deployment options and subscription terms – from self-managed to fully managed – our solutions integrate seamlessly into your identity fabric to strengthen your identity perimeter, protect against breaches, and ensure governance and compliance. title: Commvault rolls out an automated recovery mechanism, promising faster restoration of business
raw_text: Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.” Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current. Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in the organization. Commvault’s news release said that its automation allows businesses to “say goodbye to manual and painstaking attempts to restore complicated business services in a fragmented fashion that can result in downtime and data loss.” It pointed out that a large enterprise may need to restore hundreds of applications and thousands of identities, including the configurations and underlying data, all in the right order at the right time. “It’s no wonder that with conventional approaches, recovery to even a minimal level of operation takes an average of 28 days,” the release said. Commvault said Recovery Studio can manage a wide range of components that go beyond containers, VMs, files, and objects, extending to identity systems, application configurations, infrastructure configurations and security and network settings. It also promised that the Recovery Studio can standardize “across all recovery scenarios” including “operational, disaster and cyber recoveries. Unified runbooks automate infrastructure rebuilds, workload recovery, and the orchestration of security controls, such as firewall rules and network security groups and settings – all actions needed to rebuild the business, not just recover data.” The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported resources in the runbook to identify compromised areas and inform recovery decisions before returning services to production.” Commvault did not provide a spokesperson to offer further details before publication. Depends on IT awareness of the environment A number of factors will influence the effectiveness of the solution, analysts said. Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out, “nothing in Commvault’s announcement describes a generative model making recovery decisions. This is runbook automation. A runbook is a recipe: do this, then this, then this. It does not hallucinate. It does exactly what it is told.” “That is the real risk. A flawed runbook gets executed flawlessly, at machine speed,” he said. “Automation does not make a bad plan good. It makes a bad plan fast.” That means, said Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, whether Recovery Studio ultimately helps or hurts enterprise restoration efforts depends on how aware IT is of everything going on in its global footprint. “How much it solves depends on something no vendor controls, which is the accuracy of the dependency map underneath it. A runbook is a prediction about your environment and every change since it was last tested makes it a little more wrong: a new application, a rotated certificate, a firewall rule added on a Friday,” Mahapatra said. “Most enterprise dependency maps are aspirational,” he noted, “and CMDBs in particular tend to describe the environment someone intended to build. Commvault’s figure of 28 days to reach minimal operations is plausible, but the gains will go to organizations that refresh and rehearse their runbooks continuously. For everyone else, automation will execute an outdated plan faster.” Abbas Jaffery , principal advisory director at Infotech, agreed. “My concern is that automation can execute the wrong recovery sequence just as efficiently as the right one. Enterprise environments change constantly,” Jaffery said. “Applications are upgraded, infrastructure moves, identities change and integrations are added or removed. If the dependency information behind a recovery workflow is outdated, automation could restore systems successfully but leave the business service broken.” Defined recovery Mike Leone , a VP and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, added that Commvault is still advancing the space. Recovery Studio “follows defined recovery runbooks rather than a model inventing steps on the fly. That’s much more deterministic and structured,” Leone said. “Sure, automation can repeat a mistake faster than a person can, and a runbook that’s gone stale is a fair concern. But Commvault is validating each piece as it rebuilds and scanning for threats before anything goes back into production. Those are the kind of safeguards and checks everyone should want. The alternative is people rebuilding systems by hand in the middle of an outage, and that isn’t exactly mistake-free either.” But Dickson stressed that automation is not necessarily the perfect fix. “Commvault says the runbooks validate components and can scan supported resources for threats before services return to production. Good,” he said. “But the honest comparison is not automation versus perfection. It is automation versus exhausted people working from a spreadsheet at 3 a.m. Humans get the order wrong, too.” Johnny Yu , an IDC research manager, is not as impressed by the components of the solution as he is by the way Recovery Studio organizes them. “I do see Commvault Recovery Studio as significant, but not from a capability standpoint,” Yu said, adding that all of the product’s components, including recovery runbooks, threat scans, and recovery testing, are already offered by Commvault, as well as by various competitors. “I think the significance comes from how Recovery Studio organizes different recovery workflows for different applications onto a single platform or hub, kind of like a library of validated recovery runbooks to be used for all kinds of scenarios.” He explained that he liked how Studio standardizes recovery runbooks to follow a similar workflow to that of manually rebuilding the environment, recovering the components, such as data, applications and agents, and “validating the recovery before bringing it back into production, but allows recovery nuance for each runbook, such as if you want to do in-place vs secondary-site recovery or whether threat scanning is necessary, such as DR scenario vs cyber recovery scenario.” Jaffery noted, however, that while the promised Commvault cybersecurity controls are attractive, they may also be insufficient. “Following a cyberattack, organizations need to be confident they aren’t restoring compromised identities, configurations or malicious persistence mechanisms,” Jaffery said. “I would not advocate fully autonomous recovery for every scenario. There needs to be appropriate human authorization for high-impact actions, particularly those involving identity, security controls and reconnecting systems to production. And organizations need to test the entire recovery process, not just whether the backup can be restored.” An AI agent recovery plan Commvault on Tuesday also introduced AgentRecover capabilities to help track and control autonomous agents. It would specifically “help organizations audit agent activity, restore agents, and recover the data and systems they affected across environments.” Mahapatra noted that AgentRecover addresses a potentially more difficult problem than system restorations. “Restoring an agent’s configuration is straightforward. Unwinding what it did is not, because an agent’s actions land as side effects in other systems, and some of them, such as an email sent or a payment initiated, cannot be restored at all,” Mahapatra said. “Traditional recovery rolls back to a point in time,” he explained. “Rolling an environment back to 9 a.m. erases everyone’s legitimate work since 9 a.m., while rolling back only what the agent changed requires knowing causality: which agent, acting under which identity, changed which record. Commvault’s mapping of agent activity and the identities agents act through points in the right direction.” Jaffery added that rollbacks of an autonomous agent can be especially daunting. “Restoring the agent itself doesn’t necessarily undo what it has done. An agent might modify customer records, change permissions, invoke APIs or trigger downstream transactions,” he said. “You need to understand what actions it performed and what the consequences were before deciding what to reverse or restore.” Leone also noted that agents can complicate system restoration, partially because of their speed. “Agents don’t wait for anyone to confirm things are safe. The moment a system comes back, agents start hitting it, far faster than any person would,” he said. “If an agent comes back before the data and identities it relies on are verified, it starts acting on stale or incomplete information at machine speed. Get the order wrong and one outage quickly turns into a second one.” Jaffery also observed that Commvault is far from alone in the automated restoration space, and may even be a tad late. “I don’t think Commvault has an uncontested position here. Rubrik, Cohesity and Veeam have all been investing in cyber recovery, application recovery and orchestration,” he said. “Rubrik, in particular, has been pushing toward automated business application recovery and dependency mapping. Cohesity has capabilities around cyber recovery orchestration and cloud application reconstruction, while Veeam has an established disaster recovery orchestration offering.” This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .
summary: Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.” Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current. Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details.

title: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Help Device Makers Fight ‘Vulnpocalypse’ with AI-Powered Product Security
raw_text: Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates Finite State , a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices. Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure. The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains. The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it. In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability. Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch. A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see. “Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund . “Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking . “We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.” Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide. With the IoT security market projected to reach $80.3 billion by 2031, [1] Finite State’s growing international customer base reflects a challenge that increasingly transcends borders: manufacturers must understand exactly what software is inside their products, whether it can be exploited, and what they need to do about it. Bruce Lin, Senior Manager, Software Department at JET OPTOELECTRONICS CO., LTD. , a Tier 1 supplier of automotive electronics and smart cockpit solutions serving global automakers, said: “The depth of Finite State’s binary and firmware analysis, the insight it yields into what’s in a shipped device and not just the build manifest, the direct and transitive dependency visibility, and audit-ready compliance mapped to the regulations we actually face, are all invaluable.” Finite State founder and CEO Matt Wyckhouse said: “The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers. This Series C round will enable our talented team to both drive the next generation of remarkable platform advances and expand our global reach to safeguard both our customers and theirs.” Among its latest honors, Finite State was named to the 2026 Inc. 5000, an annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in America, and chosen as a finalist in SiliconANGLE’s prestigious 2026 TechForward Awards in the Security category.
