title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 63 Critical Microsoft fixes, plus an Outlook zero day that allows theft of hashed credentials
raw_text: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases. Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed. Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password. Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang , senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.” Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network. Microsoft patches Of the 1,094 Microsoft vulnerabilities, 63 were rated as critical. Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer , director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. The Windows LDAP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-119958 ) lets an unauthenticated attacker run code inside the Windows LDAP service, which puts domain controllers and the whole Active Directory environment at risk. The Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-118207 ) can be triggered by anyone able to send email to the organization, Bicer said, and the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-112967 ) gives an attacker on the same network full control of a Windows system. The fourth, the Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-119990 ), sits in a cloud service many teams now depend on. However, this service is automatically patched by Microsoft. Patch order should follow reach, not product names, Bicer advised CSOs. Domain controllers and Exchange servers go first, he said, followed by anything that exposes IIS, Microsoft Secure Channel (Schannel) or RPC to untrusted networks. Message Queuing deserves an inventory before it gets a patch: find every server where the service is enabled, turn it off where no application needs it, and patch the rest the same day, he said, adding that hypervisor hosts need their own maintenance window, because one escaped guest becomes a problem for every tenant on that host. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action,” said Dustin Childs , head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative. That means first patching Exchange and domain controllers (meaning LDAP/Kerberos) to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on cloud services your organization uses. Tyler Reguly , associate director of security R&D at Fortra, observed that there are fewer Microsoft vulnerabilities this month than there were in October, but noted, “I’m not foolish enough to think that this single drop indicates that we’re into the downward trend that I predicted we’ll see in the coming months. Instead, I think that we’re seeing a continuation of the elevated numbers as Microsoft continues to fix long hidden issues that are being surfaced by AI. Soon, however, these numbers will begin to decline as the last of these long-hidden issues are resolved and we only have new bugs to deal with.” CSOs can help their teams by ignoring any noise coming from vendors and any vulnerabilities that are overhyped, Reguly said. When vulnerability counts started to rise, it was C-level employees who jumped up the fastest and added to the burden their admins were facing. “Now it’s time to settle down and support your teams rather than increasing their burden. CSOs should keep in mind that AI companies and security vendors may needlessly hype unimportant vulnerabilities because it is cheap, effective marketing for their services,” he pointed out. “A vulnerability isn’t critical if you don’t have the impacted software deployed.” Prevention is key, so CSOs should focus their efforts on system hardening and mitigation. This, he said, will be more effective than chasing vulnerabilities. Finally, Reguly reminded CSOs that prioritization matters. “If you’ve developed a prioritization strategy that works for you, don’t change your process just because the media is looking for clicks,” he said. SAP patches The critical vulnerabilities collectively known as ICM2Shell are CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 . Researchers at Onapsis, who discovered them, said exploitation isn’t theoretical; they provided SAP with a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested. To access the flaw, an attacker only needs network access to the HTTP/HTTPS port, says Onapsis. Because WebSocket support is enabled by default in both the ICM and the SAP Web Dispatcher, a system is exposed even if no application uses WebSocket. Some services, including default ICF services in SAP S/4HANA, accept WebSocket connections without authentication, and in others the flaw can be reached before authentication takes place. “Nothing in the chain requires an SAP user, a password or a certificate,” the researchers said. The adm account owns the SAP installation, the researchers pointed out, including its executables, its instance profiles, its secure store, and its connection to the database. Running commands as that user grants full control of the SAP system. An attacker could, among other things recover database credentials and other secrets from the secure store and profiles and use them to read or alter any business data directly in the database; collect RFC destinations and technical credentials that let them move on to the SAP and non-SAP systems connected to this one; change configuration or binaries to keep persistent access; and destroy data. Other patches Chris Goettl , VP of product management at Ivanti, drew attention to patches from Adobe, Mozilla and Google. Adobe released nine security bulletins that resolve 110 CVEs, 22 of which are critical. Adobe said it is not aware of any exploits in the wild. The two Priority 2 updates carry the most risk; Connect (APSB26-191) has the largest count at 24 CVEs, 18 of them critical and six rated CVSS 10.0. The vulnerabilities span SSRF, path traversal and SQL injection, and affect Windows on-prem versions 12.12 and earlier. The Experience Manager (APSB26-189) patch fixes 14 CVEs, including four Critical code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.9. Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50, released on Monday, resolved nine CVEs including CVE-2026-125350 , which is being actively exploited in the wild. This marks Chrome’s eighth zero-day exploit of 2026, Goettl noted. Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge will need the fix as well, and users should relaunch after updating for the patch to take effect. This patched release follows Chrome 157’s November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical. Separately, Google’s November Android bulletin fixed 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them critical, with none marked as exploited. The target is patch level is 2026-11-05 or later. Mozilla’s November 10 release includes Firefox 160, which resolves 99 CVEs (57 of them are ranked High). Firefox ESR 153.7 resolves 81 vulnerabilities. (51 High), and ESR 115.45 resolves 28, all High. Many of the High-rated issues are use-after-free and memory boundary flaws across graphics, DOM, layout, and JavaScript components, including a number of sandbox escapes such as CVE-2026-124907 , a use-after-free in CanvasWebGL that allows privilege escalation and sandbox escape. The same flaw is addressed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.
summary: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases. Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024.

title: N-able N-central gets emergency fix two days after 33 exploits published
raw_text: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers. N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2 , on Tuesday. The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security. The release includes proof-of-concept exploit chains that require no authentication and could result in command execution as the service account and, in some cases, root access. N-able said it has already observed scanning activity associated with the published exploits but has not seen evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. Censys found 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances , and security firm Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication. Exploit chains lead to remote code execution The 33 exploits , which the researcher dubbed Able2Shell, are organized into four attack chains. The most severe requires no authentication and abuses an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in a service-import function to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands as the nable service user. The same chain can create a Default Administrator account with credentials chosen by the attacker, giving them full control of the appliance. Two other attack chains start from a predictable appliance passcode that lets an anonymous attacker inject malicious patch metadata. When an administrator opens the patch details, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) payload runs in their browser and invokes a command-execution interface as the nable user. The administrator’s session can also be hijacked through the same flaw to submit a crafted audit-export configuration that runs commands as root. A fourth chain writes an executable web page into the server’s web directory through a directory traversal flaw in a software repository feature, then escalates to root through a passwordless installer that executes a configuration from a directory the nable user can write to. Bales tested all of the exploits against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release build, and noted in the repository’s documentation that most, if not all, of the flaws should work on previous versions, including the most up-to-date release. N-able has not confirmed how many of the 33 flaws it could reproduce, but the new hotfix lists 7 CVEs: CVE-2026-125883 — Multiple XXE vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125878 — Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125879 — Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config CVE-2026-125880 — Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context) CVE-2026-125881 — Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation CVE-2026-125882 — RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security) CVE-2026-91000 — Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation Attacks likely to follow N-central has been targeted by attackers in the past and the Able2Shell disclosure is the fourth time in 15 months that N-able has been forced to do an emergency response. In August 2025, the company patched two flaws tracked as CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 that were exploited in the wild as zero-days. In August this year, the company patched an authentication bypass flaw tracked as CVE-2026-18556 that was exploited as a zero-day to deploy ransomware, but the patch was incomplete and attackers quickly found a bypass: CVE-2026-18577. Microsoft attributed the ransomware attacks that abused the flaw to Storm-1175, a financially motivated group linked to China that deployed the StormEncryptor ransomware on MSP-managed systems. In September, security firm Huntress discovered that a fully patched N-central server had been compromised through a new chain of access-control flaws tracked as CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207. A day later N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale that had also been exploited. N-able claims more than 25,000 MSP partners and telemetry from more than 11 million endpoints. What customers should do With the N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 available, N-able said on-premises customers should upgrade as soon as possible, and all customers — hosted and on-premises — must upgrade their Agents and Probes to restore compatibility between the two. Security firm Huntress advised N-central administrators to review authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward, look for administrator accounts, scripts, and remote-access sessions they did not create, and assess every client network managed by the server, not just the server itself. Huntress also cautioned that patched servers may not display a new version number, so administrators should verify fixes against N-able’s guidance rather than the version string. ThreatDefence recommended preserving logs and server snapshots before making any changes, then rotating credentials for administrator and technician accounts, asset-discovery databases, agent registration tokens, and ecosystem agent keys once the server is restored.
summary: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers. N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2 , on Tuesday. The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security.

title: Microsoft’s AI bug hunter finds Rust flaw that went undetected for nearly 11 years
raw_text: Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory. The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling. “The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years,” the researchers wrote in a blog post . Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. The research used Hyenas, FORGE Lab’s AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to investigate unsafe code in Rust’s standard library. Hyenas is the lab’s research version of codename MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic vulnerability-discovery system. Microsoft said some of the bugs were found with help from Hyenas. Researchers then examined the underlying code, reproduced the issues, assessed their security impact, and reported them to Rust maintainers. Microsoft said the practical risk is limited. Each flaw requires unusual conditions to trigger, and a bug in the standard library becomes “a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way,” the researchers wrote. Unsafe code challenges Rust’s safety guarantees Rust’s ownership model and type system are designed to prevent memory-safety problems commonly associated with languages such as C and C++. However, its standard library relies on unsafe code internally for operations that the compiler cannot verify. Components such as Vec and String use these operations but expose them through safe APIs. Microsoft said these APIs must meet a strict soundness requirement: “no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.” Microsoft grouped the findings into three categories: unsafe code that assumes operations will not panic, code that trusts user-provided implementations to behave correctly, and code that makes incorrect assumptions about the underlying system. The first involved a panic-safety problem in Rust’s MapWindows::clone implementation. The function created a buffer before fully initializing its contents and then called a user-provided clone operation to populate it. If that operation triggered a panic, Rust’s unwinding mechanism could invoke the buffer’s destructor, which would attempt to access uninitialized memory. Microsoft said the reported fix prevents the partially initialized buffer from being destroyed before initialization is complete. Another finding involved str::replace. The researchers found that the function could make an incorrect assumption about a custom implementation of the nightly Pattern trait. A custom implementation could supply a non-ASCII byte where the code expected an ASCII character, causing the replacement operation to produce invalid UTF-8 data. Subsequent string operations could then trigger undefined behavior, Microsoft said. System-level bugs affect stable Rust Microsoft said the first two categories of weaknesses were already being studied in 2021 through Rudra, a static analyzer developed by members of the research team. The standard library had also addressed panic-safety problems as far back as 2015, but similar weaknesses continue to appear in its implementations. The third category involves interactions between Rust and underlying operating systems and C libraries. Besides the process::exit issue, researchers identified a problem in Rust’s CommandExt::exec functionality involving the process-wide environment variable array. Microsoft found that the function could modify this shared state while holding a read lock, potentially allowing other threads to access inconsistent data. Under certain conditions, concurrent operations could leave the environment pointer referencing freed memory. Microsoft said both the process::exit and CommandExt::exec findings affect stable Rust. A proposed fix for the environment-variable issue, which avoids modifying the shared array by calling execve directly, was under review when the blog was published. Two issues reported by Microsoft’s team remained open at publication. The blog also discussed related reports from other researchers and fixes still under review. Findings feed into Microsoft’s security products Microsoft said the research findings can also feed into Microsoft Perception, its multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work across broader security workflows. It would therefore help the company improve the development of MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. For example, Microsoft’s Web App Pen Test Agent can use MDASH findings to prioritize testing, assess exploitability against live applications, and provide information to support remediation, the researchers wrote. “Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs,” the researchers wrote, but to identify meaningful issues and improve the safety of foundational software developers and organizations depend on. The Rust project had not responded to a request for comment from CSO at the time of writing.
summary: Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory. The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running.

title: Qubole supply chain attack exposed AWS, Entra ID, and Okta credentials
raw_text: An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26. Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments. The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3 , and test credentials belonging to affected organizations. Sentra, which initially identified suspicious activity across several customer environments, said the campaign affected dozens of Qubole customers. The attacker was said to have exploited integrations that remained trusted even after some organizations had stopped using the platform. Attackers used Qubole’s AWS credentials Qubole integrations rely on cross-account Identity and Access Management ( IAM ) roles. Customers typically create roles that allow identities belonging to Qubole’s AWS account to assume them, with an External ID serving as an additional check against unauthorized access. The attacker had credentials that could satisfy this requirement. Wiz said the first suspicious activity was observed on October 14, when an IP address associated with Mullvad VPN attempted to assume customer integration roles from AWS account 805246085872, which Qubole uses for its platform operations. The requests used an IAM user identified as AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Most of the activity that came later originated from an OVH-hosted VPS, 57.129.54[.]120. The attacker also began using a second IAM identity associated with Qubole’s AWS account on October 18, alongside another Mullvad VPN address. All malicious role-assumption requests identified by Wiz included the required External ID and succeeded. Many of the targeted roles had seen no legitimate Qubole activity during October, but their permissions remained active. After gaining access, the attacker enumerated cloud resources, including S3 buckets, databases, EC2 instances, security groups and IAM identities. The intruder also accessed AWS Secrets Manager, Systems Manager Parameter Store and Lambda function configurations to retrieve credentials and other sensitive information. Attackers stole data, and hosted a suspicious Linux image The attacker used the assumed roles to download data from Amazon S3, enumerating accessible buckets and objects before retrieving their contents. In some instances, Wiz said, entire buckets were downloaded in individual sessions. Credentials discovered in the compromised environments were subsequently tested using TruffleHog, a secrets-scanning tool. These included AWS access keys, Microsoft Entra ID service principal credentials and Okta OAuth client credentials. Sentra reported identifying more than 100 passwords and keys read within minutes, alongside thousands of additional credential records contained in downloaded files. The company also said the attacker performed no write operations in the observed environments, suggesting an operation focused on data theft. Wiz also found a bootable Linux ISO image, named “sso_agent.iso,” hosted on the attacker’s OVH infrastructure. The image collects system information, communicates with the server over TCP port 23458, and can execute remotely supplied shell commands. Its configuration suggests it may have been designed to target Windows systems, the researchers said in a blog post . Wiz, however, did not find any deployments of the image and could not confirm whether it had been used against victims. The campaign has not been attributed to a known threat group. Tightening integrations and third-party access will help Wiz recommends that organizations using Qubole review AWS CloudTrail records dating back to October 1, 2026, across all accounts containing integration roles. Investigators should look for suspicious AssumeRole activity originating from Qubole’s AWS account, particularly requests from non-AWS infrastructure and IAM identities identified in the disclosure. Subsequent activity involving Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Lambda and S3 should also be investigated, Wiz noted. Other recommendations include removing unused third-party integrations and narrowing trust policies to specific vendor IAM principals rather than allowing an entire external AWS account to assume a role. Organizations should also restrict role assumption to documented vendor network ranges using AWS source IP or VPC endpoint conditions.
summary: An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26. Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments. The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3 , and test credentials belonging to affected organizations.

title: Anthropic sharpens AI coding and security capabilities with Mythos 5.2
raw_text: Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse. The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively. Anthropic said the newer versions can generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors. The company reported substantial gains in coding performance. Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at its Xhigh effort setting, compared with 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The benchmark assesses whether maintainers of open-source projects would accept AI-generated changes to their code. Performance and costs could entice enterprises The models’ improved performance and lower prices could make long-running AI agents viable for software migrations and scientific research, according to Lian Jye Su , chief analyst at Omdia. Higher task completion rates could further reduce deployment costs, he said. Anthropic said Fable 5.2 at its “High effort” setting achieved a coding benchmark score comparable to Opus 5.5 at its highest setting, at roughly half the cost per task. The comparison suggests that Fable could be more economical for some demanding assignments, although the savings would depend on the workload and effort setting. “Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a thought,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research. He urged CIOs to treat AI processing effort as a budget consideration and measure costs against successfully completed tasks. Anthropic also recommends Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, with Fable and Mythos intended for more demanding assignments. Reliability challenges persist In an internal experiment, an Anthropic engineer tasked Fable 5.2 with building a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced software that could boot on a laptop. Su said the improvements bring enterprises closer to highly autonomous software development, although widespread deployment will depend on addressing persistent operational limitations. “Reliability remains an issue without human supervision,” Su said. Coordinating multiple AI agents across enterprise tools and internal teams also remains difficult, he added. Organizations will need to monitor agent activity and run these systems in appropriately isolated environments. Critical changes should remain subject to human approval , with sufficient visibility into agent behavior to support audits. Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said complex legacy systems and the need to meet business requirements could limit how much software development enterprises can delegate to AI agents. Faster vulnerability discovery raises concerns Anthropic said Mythos 5.2 identified 89.6% of vulnerabilities in its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1. Conducted against 1,829 previously disclosed vulnerabilities, the test assessed whether models could independently rediscover flaws in software snapshots taken before the vulnerabilities were fixed. The company said Mythos 5.2 was also better at reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes. Anthropic has restricted direct access to Mythos 5.2 through its verification programs. However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said. According to Su, “Mythos 5.2 shifts the balance towards defenders in controlled enterprise settings.” Jain, however, cautioned that advances in AI-powered vulnerability discovery could also help attackers identify software weaknesses more quickly. “This creates an AI-powered race between attackers and defenders,” he said. Data retention raises compliance questions Anthropic said customers eligible for zero data retention can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 under those arrangements, while other customers face 30-day retention for safety monitoring. The company has also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, currently in private beta, which allows automated safety monitoring to run on prompts and responses stored within customers’ infrastructure. Gogia said data retention requirements could outweigh the benefits of lower API prices for regulated enterprises. He urged procurement teams to obtain written confirmation of zero-retention arrangements before deploying the models for sensitive workloads. The article originally appeared on InfoWorld .
summary: Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse. The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively.

title: When everything is a threat, nothing feels safe
raw_text: When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them. Our digital lives are different. We shop, bank, work and keep in touch with family and friends online, often without clear signs of where a danger begins or which precaution matters most. We receive a steady stream of warnings about new scams, stolen credentials, data breaches and software vulnerabilities. The messages vary in urgency, but many seem to demand our immediate attention. The result can be an uncomfortable contradiction: information intended to make us safer can also leave us overwhelmed and less willing to act. In conversations with people inside and outside the technology field, I keep hearing variations of the same concerns. There is a new scam every week, and no way to keep up. If major companies can be breached, how can an individual protect themselves? Almost anything done online seems risky. These are reasonable questions. As a cybersecurity professional, I believe our response should go beyond repeating that threats exist. We need to help people understand which risks are relevant, what they can do about them and where their responsibility ends. When a warning becomes background noise There are good reasons to monitor the threat landscape. Criminals adapt their techniques, fraud schemes evolve and vulnerabilities sometimes require urgent remediation. Ignoring those developments is not a sensible strategy. But a threat’s existence is not the same as a person’s or organization’s exposure to it. A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business. The answer depends on which products are in use, whether affected systems are exposed, what safeguards are already in place and the potential business impact. A critical flaw in technology that an organization does not use may be worth noting without requiring emergency action. A less dramatic issue affecting a business-critical, internet-facing service could deserve immediate attention. The headline alone cannot make that distinction. Yet headlines are often how people encounter cybersecurity. When warnings arrive without context, prioritization or practical guidance, they compete for a limited amount of attention. What should be exceptional starts to feel routine. An alert that genuinely requires action may disappear into the noise. There is a meaningful difference between staying informed and feeling compelled to remain on high alert every moment of the day. Security fatigue is not simply a lack of interest Researchers have a name for part of this experience: security fatigue . In a 2016 qualitative study, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) interviewed 40 everyday computer users about security and privacy . Signs of fatigue appeared in 25 interviews, even though fatigue was not the study’s initial focus. Participants described frustration with repeated requirements and advice, along with feelings of resignation and diminished control. The researchers connected these experiences with decision avoidance, choosing the easiest option available, and disregarding protective guidance. The study was small and qualitative, so it should not be treated as a measure of how widespread fatigue is today. Its value lies in explaining behavior that security teams may otherwise label as carelessness. When someone dismisses yet another warning, they may not be indifferent to security. They may simply have lost the ability to tell what matters, what is urgent and what action is expected of them. This distinction matters for security leaders. If every message is marked urgent, we should not be surprised when urgency stops working. More warnings are not automatically better communication. Replace headline volume with decision criteria I do not believe people need to memorize every new phishing technique or follow every vulnerability disclosure to practice sound digital security. Nor is it sustainable for security teams to treat every issue as equally important. A better approach starts with three questions whenever a new alert appears: 1. Does this affect me or my organization? Is the alert about a service, device, account or process I use or oversee? 2. Does it require action now? Is there credible guidance and a concrete reason for urgency, or is this general information about a possible threat? 3. What is the most effective action available to me? Should I install an update, verify an unusual request through another channel, enable a safeguard or notify the appropriate team? This is not a guarantee of safety. It is a way to separate useful information from noise and preserve attention for decisions that matter. For individuals, a consistent baseline is more valuable than trying to recognize the scam of the week: keep devices and applications updated, use long and unique passwords with a password manager, enable multifactor authentication and verify requests that demand immediate action or sensitive information. These habits are easy to describe, even if implementing them sometimes requires help. For organizations, the equivalent is a risk-based process that connects alerts to actual assets, exposure, business priorities and clear owners. A security bulletin should answer who is affected, what the organization knows, what needs to happen and by when. When no action is required, saying so is also useful. The burden cannot rest entirely on users It would be unfair to finish this discussion by giving people another long list of obligations. If staying secure requires every employee to interpret technical warnings, navigate confusing settings and make the correct choice every time, the design of the system is part of the problem. Organizations and technology providers should make secure behavior easier by default. That includes sensible protective settings, automated updates where appropriate, effective filtering, straightforward reporting channels and clear instructions when a real decision is necessary. It also means preparing for mistakes through detection, response and recovery rather than assuming flawless human behavior. NIST’s work on human-centered cybersecurity makes a similar case : systems and guidance should account for people’s actual needs, capabilities and limitations. The goal is to make safe actions easier to take in practice, not merely to issue more instructions. Security leaders can put that principle to work by reviewing the warnings employees receive. Are several teams sending overlapping messages about the same threat? Do alerts explain the action and its owner? Are we asking employees to solve problems that technical control could prevent? Can people report a suspicious message without fearing blame? These questions recognize that user behavior matters, but it always takes place within a system that can support or undermine good decisions. Build awareness through confidence I want security awareness to treat people as partners, not as the weakest link to be frightened into compliance. Good risk communication should explain why something matters, whom it affects and what realistic next step is available. It should also be able to say when there is no reason to panic. Confidence does not mean assuming nothing will go wrong. It means understanding the most relevant risks, knowing which protections are in place and knowing where to turn when something unusual happens. We should therefore be careful about how we measure awareness. The number of alerts distributed, or training messages delivered tells us little about whether people can act on what they have learned. I would rather ask a more demanding question: After receiving our guidance, are people better equipped to make a sound decision? If the answer is no, we need to change how we communicate cybersecurity. Awareness should not be about frightening people. It should provide knowledge, a sense of control and practical ways to act.
summary: When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them.

title: SonicWall releases patches for 7 flaws in its firewalls, most involving unauthenticated access
raw_text: SonicWall on Monday updated its advisory about seven cybersecurity holes affecting its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls, five of which allow unauthenticated remote attacks, to warn that it is aware of “potential” active exploitation of at least one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868, a bypass of SAML authentication controls in its SonicOS SSL VPN service. And Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out that these flaws involve different SonicWall product lines to those recently reported . “The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said. “This one hits SonicOS, the operating system on its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls. The pattern has jumped product lines. That makes it a vendor issue, not a product issue. Credit where due: SonicWall flagged the exploitation report in its own advisory and the fix shipped with the disclosure.” The seven vulnerabilities are: CVE-2026-107155, a permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability, with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-107154, a session validation vulnerability, also with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-82308, a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in SSL-VPN, with a CVSS score of 7.5; CVE-2026-19868, an authentication enforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods, with a CVSS score of 7.1; CVE-2026-77708, a pre-authentication stack buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of 5.9; CVE-2026-77709 , a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of also 5.9; and CVE-2026-19703, a weak password hashing hole with a CVSS score of 5.2. SonicWall only provided a workaround for one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868; it involves disabling or deleting any active LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall. A ‘mixed bag’ Dickson said the newly reported holes are a mixed bag. “SonicWall’s advisory rates its SAML bypass, CVE-2026-19868, a 7.1, below two 8.8 management interface flaws,” Dickson said. “Yet it is the one CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day SonicWall disclosed it. SonicWall describes ‘potential exploitation’ but CISA says active. I would listen to CISA.” The bug lets anyone holding valid credentials for another login method, such as a local account or LDAP, skip SAML and the MFA that rides on it, he noted, adding “companies moved their VPNs to SAML precisely so every login passes through the identity provider and its MFA prompt. This flaw breaks that promise.” Some of the other authentication holes are potentially less severe, however. “Three are pre-authentication buffer overflows whose stated impact is denial of service. They knock the VPN offline but they do not open it,” Dickson said. “The two 8.8 flaws work only under specific conditions. None of the six is known to be exploited. They matter, [but] they are not the headline.” Could be combined Sav Wheeler , malware research engineer at Malwarebytes, added that even though some of these holes do not appear to be especially serious on their own, they could be combined to be much more dangerous. “These scattered vulnerabilities at various stages of the authentication process combine to form a pathway where an attacker can bypass authentication almost entirely to penetrate a system and steal credentials,” Wheeler said. “The weak password hashing is a cherry on top for attackers that have already gained an initial foothold.” He sees CVE-2026-19868 as “the biggest individual vulnerability” because the potential MFA bypass through alternative authentication means that “the entire trust boundary of MFA could be effectively nonexistent even when an organization depends on it for security.” He noted, however, that although the attacker does need valid credentials for an alternate authentication method for this to work, “otherwise it requires little effort and resources to gain access, as they’re not compromising the MFA itself. Combined with the use of IP addresses for validation (CVE-2026-107154), which itself provides little security, this is a serious failure of authentication policy to ensure a user is who they claim to be.” Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said that the biggest danger is when SAML sits atop older directory logins that stay live. “Remote access is the lifeblood of a distributed business, and one stolen directory password now reaches it. CISOs who rolled out SAML to end password-only access have cause to feel let down. SonicWall owes them a full account of how the second path stayed open.” A vendor risk management issue These continuing SonicWall vulnerabilities are a real issue, although the September and October flaws sit in another product, Gogia said. “Those hit the SMA1000 remote-access gateway, while this advisory covers SonicOS firewalls. But thirteen of SonicWall’s twenty entries in CISA’s exploited list carry the flag for known ransomware use, the highest share among eight edge vendors.” Dickson noted that the next steps for enterprise CISOs are trickier because the fault here might lie less with a vendor than with the product category itself. “The internet-facing VPN appliance is the Achilles’ heel of the perimeter, whoever builds it,” he pointed out. “Swapping vendors swaps one heel for another. The pattern should change how CISOs deploy the edge, not just whose logo is on it. Ask SonicWall whether these are new bugs or the same bug classes coming back.” However Erik Avakian , technical counselor at Infotech, said he was less willing to let SonicWall off the hook that easily. “Any vendor can and is generally going to experience vulnerabilities, but when we see repeated critical security issues affecting the same vendor that represent a pattern, particularly involving authentication and internet-facing infrastructure, it raises legitimate questions about their secure development practices, quality assurance, and the effectiveness of their own internal vulnerability management processes,” Avakian said. “At some point, this becomes more than just an individual vulnerability management issue. It becomes a vendor risk management issue.” He noted that CISOs need to evaluate whether the frequency and severity of these vulnerabilities are creating an unacceptable level of recurring exposure for their organization. “That doesn’t automatically mean replacing SonicWall products, but it does require holding the vendor accountable for improvement and to demonstrate their ability to address the underlying problems,” he said. Additional preventive measures In addition, Dickson suggested other ways CISOs can protect themselves in light of these new holes, beyond the obvious step of patching them. “List every way the VPN can authenticate a user: local accounts, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+. Delete what you do not need, especially leftover local admin and service accounts. Rotate passwords on every non-SAML account that remains,” he advised. “Compare VPN logins against identity provider sign-ins. A VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in is your red flag. Look back as far as your logs go, since SonicWall has not said when exploitation began. And take the management interface off the open internet.”

title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
raw_text: Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones. Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN. The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post. The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.” Intermittent sending issues DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing , and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes. But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected. For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum : Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered. hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location. Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. A Microsoft external staff moderator called it a “service degradation” currently under active investigation. According to email security company MailRoute , enterprises can determine if their domain is impacted with this command on any terminal (replacing example.com with their domain): dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com . A response starting with v=DMARC1 means there is a DMARC record; no reply means there isn’t, MailRoute said. The fix is a single TXT record: v=DMARC1 ; p=none . This declares that a domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures, MailRoute explained. DMARC meant to make impersonation difficult DMARC relies on two foundational email authentication tools that must be active on a domain: SPF and DKIM. SPF verifies whether the sending server’s IP address is allowed to send email on behalf of a domain, while DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message to prove it wasn’t altered along the way and actually belongs to the domain it says it is coming from. DMARC checks the two, identifying whether the domain listed on the “from” address aligns with the validated domains. It ties those checks to the name the reader actually sees and tells receivers what to do with forgeries, Dickson explained. “Without it, impersonating your domain is easy,” he said. “That is where a lot of phishing and business email compromise starts.” But because Microsoft, at least to this point, has only required DMARC for larger senders, it is not standard across the board; many small senders reasonably concluded it did not apply to them, Dickson noted. This includes SMBs, nonprofits, schools, and professional practices such as law firms, accountants, and doctors’ offices running on domains that “someone set up years ago, and nobody has touched since.” Larger organizations miss DMARC on secondary domains, regional domains, and the subdomains that their marketing and billing platforms send from for mundane reasons. No one owns the domain name system (DNS), and “people fear breaking legitimate mail sent by third parties,” Dickson said. Quiet, inconsistent failure As MailRoute pointed out, what makes this particular malfunction so dangerous is its inconsistency: The person who sent the message sees a bounce “full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on.” Meanwhile, the customer never knows a message was sent. It fails quietly, which is “the bane of an email marketer’s existence,” Dickson said. Customers, patients, job applicants, and others use Hotmail, Outlook, Live, and MSN, and when invoices, password resets, appointment confirmations, and offer letters go missing, the customer thinks they’re being ignored, not necessarily that the message is not getting through. The good news is that the failures are findable, he pointed out. Every rejection generated a bounce, and bounces are logged. Enterprises should search mail logs, email platforms’ bounce reports, and help desk tickets for entries citing “ Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC ” since Nov. 5. Then, resend what matters, time-sensitive transactional mail first. From there, fix the cause by confirming that every domain sending mail as you publishes a DMARC record, Dickson advised. If one is missing, a basic monitoring record (p=none) stops these bounces without changing how anyone else treats your mail, as long as SPF or DKIM lines up with the From domain. Microsoft 365 customers who never turned on DKIM for their own domains should do it now, he advised. “Do not rewrite SPF just because the bounce blames it,” he said. If your records are clean and mail still bounces, send the full bounce to Microsoft so it lands in the investigation. However, a p=none record is “first base, not home plate,” he said. The goal is p=reject , which tells receivers to refuse anyone forging your name. Inventory every service that sends email as you, Dickson advised: The CRM, the billing system, the HR platform, and the marketing tools. “Most organizations cannot produce that list,” he noted. “You cannot protect a domain when you do not know who is speaking for it.” A signal of what is to come While it remains to be seen what is causing this glitch, enterprises should make no mistake about where things are heading, Dickson said: DMARC will be enforced for every sender. Google and Yahoo began requiring it of bulk senders in February 2024; Microsoft followed in May 2025. “Requirements start with the big senders and then become the floor for everyone,” he said. “The rollout was botched, but the destination is not in doubt.” But while Microsoft has the destination right, “nobody should learn about a new rule from a bounce message.” Update Nov. 10: On Tuesday, Microsoft issued a statement saying that the issue, related to an update to its spam rules, has been resolved. Users do not need to adjust any settings or take additional action. A Microsoft spokesperson said, “ We’ve resolved an issue that may have prevented some email messages from reaching Outlook.com, Hotmail and Live addresses, and mail flow has been restored. We’re continuing to monitor to help ensure email is delivered as expected. Customers can learn more via EX1545193 in the Microsoft 365 admin center. “ This article originally appeared on Computerworld .
summary: Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones. Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN. The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time .

title: MWC26 Doha: Qatar positions itself as a global technology hub
raw_text:
Qatar is looking to turn its growing investments in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and technology innovation into a platform for international growth, as the country seeks to establish itself as a regional technology hub and expand the global reach of its digital businesses.

The ambition was a key theme at MWC26 Doha, where government officials, telecommunications operators and technology leaders gathered to discuss the future of connectivity and the digital economy across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA).

Held in partnership with Qatar’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), the second edition of MWC Doha at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Centre brought together the mobile industry and the International Telecommunication Union’s (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference.

The event comes as mobile technology’s economic contribution across MENA continues to grow. According to the GSMA’s Mobile Economy MENA 2026 report, mobile technologies and services generated $380bn in economic value across the region in 2025, equivalent to 5.8% of regional GDP. This figure is forecast to reach $470bn by 2030.

For Qatar, the opportunity extends beyond expanding domestic connectivity. The country wants to develop an ecosystem that can produce and export digital services, software and technology solutions to international markets, while strengthening its position as a technology and innovation centre for the wider region.

From digital infrastructure to digital exports

During the event, officials from MCIT highlighted how the country’s National Digital Development Strategy is placing digital exports at the centre of its economic diversification ambitions.

The strategy aims to increase the contribution of the digital economy from approximately QR7bn in 2025 to QR11.6bn, while growing the digital sector’s contribution and improving Qatar’s access to major international markets.

The ministry’s representatives argued that digital exports could create a multiplier effect across the economy. As domestic companies develop products and services for international customers, they are likely to increase their investment in technology, strengthen their digital capabilities and generate further demand for ICT services.

This creates what ministry officials described as a digital export flywheel, in which successful international expansion drives further innovation, investment and growth across the technology sector.

The opportunity covers two broad areas: digitally delivered services, including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, fintech and digital content; and digitally ordered products sold through online platforms. However, Qatar still has considerable ground to cover before it can fully capitalise on this opportunity.

According to figures presented by MCIT, Qatar’s digitally delivered services market was valued at approximately QR4.3bn in 2023, representing around 0.56% of the global market. The country’s share of digitally ordered products was also relatively small.

More broadly, digital imports remain approximately 2.2 times higher than digital exports, highlighting the gap between domestic demand for technology and the ability of Qatari companies to compete internationally.

The comparison with other markets illustrates the scale of the opportunity. Ministry officials highlighted Singapore, where digital exports account for approximately 36% of the relevant economic activity, compared with around 9% in both the UAE and France, and approximately 2% in Qatar.

Closing that gap will require more than investment in infrastructure. It will mean helping domestic companies develop export-ready products, connecting them with international buyers, improving cross-border payment and delivery systems, and reducing the operational barriers associated with entering foreign markets.

Qatar has already established support mechanisms, including its Qatar Digital Export Support Programme and the Scale Now initiative, which aims to mentor, advise and connect local businesses with regional and international opportunities.

The ministry highlighted that 225 startups already have international exposure, while Qatar’s export support ecosystem has assisted more than 400 exporters and delivered 178 workshops and training sessions.

Nevertheless, officials identified several challenges, including uneven business maturity, limited access to foreign markets, high cross-border operating costs and difficulties in scaling products beyond Qatar.

Government investment at the heart of Qatar’s AI ambitions

Artificial intelligence (AI) is another important component of Qatar’s ambitions to become a global technology hub, with the government taking a central role in establishing the infrastructure and conditions required to accelerate adoption.

Speaking during the MWC26 Doha discussion, H.E. Reem Mohammed Al Mansoori, assistant undersecretary for digital industry affairs at MCIT, outlined how Qatar is approaching AI as a national transformation programme rather than a conventional technology deployment.

She described the speed of AI development as a significant challenge for government organisations, explaining that technologies that were still being considered during programme planning 18 months earlier had since become readily available.

“It developed so quickly, so fast. So what we were thinking 18 months back, today it becomes available, easy to implement,” she said.

This pace of change has required Qatar to adopt a more agile approach to government technology programmes, including working closely with international technology companies and implementation partners.

Al Mansoori argued that governments cannot leave AI infrastructure investment entirely to the private sector, given the scale of the resources required and the importance of making these capabilities accessible across the wider economy.

“With AI, the ecosystem cannot be replicated as previous technology has been growing and organically developed. With AI, everyone needs to work closely. The government needs to be at the heart of that,” she added.

She highlighted the importance of investing in datacentres, computing capacity, graphics processing units (GPUs) and shared services to enable organisations to develop and deploy AI applications without shouldering the full cost of the underlying infrastructure.

In Qatar, initiatives involving AI infrastructure, GPU capacity and shared digital services are intended to provide a common foundation on which government entities and private sector organisations can build their own use cases.

This approach reflects a broader ambition to make Qatar an attractive destination for AI development, enterprise innovation and technology investment.

However, Al Mansoori stressed that infrastructure alone would not guarantee successful AI adoption. Organisations must understand how AI can fundamentally change their operations, rather than simply using it to automate existing processes or reduce costs.

“You cannot just replicate any system with AI. You cannot just try to make any job effective just by using AI,” she said.

Instead, she argued that AI initiatives must be led by organisational leadership, supported by clear business objectives, and accompanied by change management and workforce reskilling.

Al Mansoori highlighted executive training programmes introduced in Qatar to help business and government leaders understand how AI could transform their organisations. The programmes have also evolved to encourage participants to bring forward real business use cases and develop plans for implementing them.

She emphasised that leadership readiness is critical to successful AI adoption, with employees at every level needing to understand how the technology will change their roles and the way organisations operate.

Connectivity and regional cooperation

Qatar’s digital ambitions are developing alongside a wider transformation of the telecommunications sector across MENA, where investment in next-generation networks is expected to support new industries, services and business models.

The GSMA forecasts that 5G connections will increase from 9% of the region’s total mobile connections in 2025 to 40% by 2030. Mobile operators are expected to invest $88.9bn over the same period.

Yet the region continues to face a significant connectivity challenge. Although 48% of the MENA population used mobile internet in 2025, a further 49% remained offline despite living in areas covered by mobile broadband networks.

This usage gap highlights the need to focus not only on network deployment, but also on affordability, digital skills, relevant services and the ability of businesses and citizens to benefit from connectivity.

At MWC26 Doha, GSMA director general Vivek Badrinath emphasised the importance of maintaining global industry standards and extending connectivity to underserved populations. “Progress only counts if everyone shares in it,” he said, highlighting the need for standards that ensure networks, services and devices remain interoperable across borders.

The next phase of Qatar’s digital transformation will therefore depend on its ability to connect infrastructure investment with commercial opportunities.

Building datacentres, expanding AI capabilities and improving connectivity will establish the foundations. But turning those investments into internationally competitive businesses will require stronger export capabilities, access to global markets, skilled talent and a supportive regulatory environment.

title: Data dive: Mapping UK councils’ hyperscale dependence
raw_text:
It’s not going to surprise anyone that the UK’s 382 councils are heavily dependent on US-based hyperscalers. In this article, we map the exact dependence via the digital perimeter those councils expose – the mail servers, web front ends and cloud endpoints that appear in a public domain name system (DNS) – and find that more than half their routable infrastructure points to Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google, with Microsoft the dominant player.

The scan covers 382 local authorities across all four nations: 317 in England, 32 in Scotland, 22 in Wales and 11 in Northern Ireland. We resolved 46,822 DNS records across their 394 principal domains and, for each address, identified the network owner through public registration data. Each record is a signal that points to where a council’s services actually live.

The picture is near-universal dependence. Of the domains studied, 390 of 394 (99%) route at least one record to Microsoft, AWS or Google. Of the records that route to a real destination, 51% sit on one of those three providers. Microsoft alone accounts for 13,473 of the 19,407 records that reach a hyperscaler – roughly seven in 10.

The finding continues a pattern Computer Weekly has mapped across the public sector. Earlier data dives found the same gravitational pull at the NHS, in police forces and across central government. What changes at council level is the reach. Authorities that run everything from council tax portals to children’s services have moved the public face of those services onto the same handful of providers.

TL;DR – UK councils secure but very dependent on US cloud

  • 382 UK councils’ public DNS was mapped – 46,822 records across 394 domains.
  • 51% of routable records sit on Microsoft, Amazon or Google; 99% of councils touch at least one hyperscaler.
  • Microsoft alone accounts for seven in 10 hyperscaler records – 338 councils lean primarily on it.
  • 99.7% publish a DMARC anti-spoofing policy, with 60% rejecting outright.
  • Germany keeps 87% of council email domestic but publishes DMARC far less; Britain is the mirror image.

    How we mapped it

    Every council publishes, in its DNS, where its mail goes and which cloud services host its websites. We read only that public record – no internal systems, no authentication.

    For each council, we gathered records through encrypted DNS lookups, certificate-transparency logs and a dictionary of common public service subdomains. We then resolved every address to its registered owner using the iptoasn bulk IP-to-ASN database, which maps network ranges to the organisations that hold them. Where an owner is Microsoft, Amazon or Google, the record counts as hyperscaler; Cloudflare and Akamai are treated as content delivery networks, not hyperscalers. Records that resolve to no address are excluded and, because they can only add to the totals, the hyperscaler share is a lower bound.

    The Microsoft pull

    Microsoft is the centre of gravity. Of the records that touch a hyperscaler, 13,473 are Microsoft, 5,438 Amazon and 496 Google – a ratio of roughly 2.5:1 against AWS and 27:1 against Google. The pull is starkest when councils are ordered by their primary provider. Of 390 councils with a hyperscaler link, 338 lean primarily on Microsoft, 47 on AWS and just five on Google.

    The same concentration shows at the sharp end. The London Borough of Hackney reaches 222 distinct hyperscaler addresses across its public estate; Leeds 126, Merton 87, Southwark 84, and Kensington and Chelsea 73.

    The range of entanglement is wide. Plymouth City Council’s public DNS fans out across Microsoft, AWS, Google, Capita, Cloudflare and Apple, alongside infrastructure it still runs itself. Maidstone Borough Council, by contrast, routes a clean set of a few subdomains to Microsoft and little else – a reminder that “on the cloud” can mean many things.

    Some councils keep a measure of control. Birmingham, Coventry, Warwickshire, Bristol and Plymouth all still hold visible chunks of on-premise infrastructure, even though the bulk of their footprint sits with hyperscalers.

    The security twist

    The same councils that have concentrated infrastructure on US providers have adopted email anti-spoofing at a rate that puts much of Europe to shame. Our independent check of the councils’ DMARC records found 99.7% publish a policy, with 60% set to reject failing mail outright and a further 36% quarantining it. That is near-total adoption of the control that stops criminals from forging a council’s domain.

    Set that against the continent, and the contrast sharpens. In the most recent published measurement of German, Austrian and Swiss municipalities – a peer-reviewed study covering more than 15,000 domains – only 50.7% of German councils published a DMARC record, with the equivalent figure being 37.4% in Austria and 55.5% in Switzerland. Strict enforcement is rare in all three, from 3% to 17%. Having said that, Germany, unlike the UK, keeps its email largely at home. Some 87% of its municipalities use domestic providers, whereas 67% in Austria and 52% in Switzerland run on Microsoft.

    Britain, in other words, has strong security but deep dependence. Germany has greater sovereignty but left the controls half-built. Austria and Switzerland have managed the worst of both – concentrated on US cloud and stayed weak on enforcement.

    Dependence this deep on a single provider is a resilience question as much as a security one. Strong controls protect mail, but they do not answer what happens to a council’s services if its one supplier stumbles, raises prices or is drawn into a geopolitical dispute.

title: Post Office to reach ‘milestone’ and eventually dump Fujitsu by September 2027
raw_text:
Fujitsu will begin handing over its Post Office operation to Accenture in the summer of next year, with one more contract extension before its autumn exit.

The final day for Fujitsu is 1 September 2027 at the latest, according to the Post Office, which will require a six-month extension to the current £40m 12-month deal that ends in March. The final hard date, which will end a 30-year relationship, will be announced then.

As revealed by Computer Weekly last month, an extension of the current deal was on the cards. This is now confirmed.

“A short, time-limited contract extension has also been agreed to facilitate the transition process,” said the Post Office.

In May, Accenture won a £322.8m contract to run Horizon, while the electronic point of sale (EPOS) system from OneView Commerce was chosen in a £169m deal.

There have been delays. As revealed by Computer Weekly, Escher threatened legal action after its bid to win the EPOS replacement contract failed. The EPOS contract was agreed with OneView in May, and was originally set to be formally signed off at the beginning of June, but it was delayed six times due to extensions to the standoff period.

Amid the Escher challenge, on 7 August, the Post Office created a new contract and awarded it directly to the supplier. This contract is for Escher’s proprietary Product Journey Engine. Taxpayers will pay £14m in its first year for development and configuration. Licensing and support for later years will be separately procured.

Read more: Post Office Horizon scandal explained: Everything you need to know

On the Fujitsu exit deadline, Post Office CEO Neil Brocklehurst said: “Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone in Post Office’s transformation, and today’s agreement secures the transition away from Fujitsu and over to Accenture safely and responsibly to achieve our target of summer 2027.

“In addition to ending our contract with Fujitsu, we are also working at pace with our leading technology suppliers, Accenture, OneView Commerce and Escher, to build a modern, resilient platform able to make everyday life easier for customers and postmasters for years to come,” he said.

Subpostmaster and Post Office non-executive director Sara Barlow said: “For me, appointing the new suppliers felt like a genuine milestone. It represented an opportunity to learn from the past while building something better for the future. There is still a lot of work ahead, but it is encouraging to see the focus on getting this right.”

Read more: Fujitsu’s role in the Post Office scandal: Everything you need to know

The Horizon replacement project was first planned almost exactly seven years ago, after the Post Office admitted defeat in the Alan Bates and Others versus Post Office group litigation, when it was proved Horizon errors caused the account shortfalls that subpostmasters were blamed and punished for. But nothing really moved, and it was only after the ITV dramatisation of the Post Office scandal in January 2024, amid public outrage, that things started to happen.

This culminated in the £1.8bn New Branch IT project, but this ran into trouble and was eventually axed in May 2024, and was replaced by the current project.

There have been multiple Fujitsu extensions worth nearly £200m since 2019, but the next will be the last.

Computer Weekly first exposed the scandal in 2009, with the stories of seven subpostmasters.

title: Gartner Symposium: Who is in control of AI?
raw_text:
The second day keynote at the Gartner Symposium in Barcelona featured a conversation with historian Yuval Noah Harari, co-founder of social impact company Sapienship.

The discussion is something that may colour organisations’ technology strategies relating to how and where artificial intelligence (AI) fits, and what the direction of travel of the tech sector points to.

The keynote questioned whether CEOs of the AI giants truly appreciate that they may be developing “god-like” capabilities with AI that humankind would be unable to control.

Unlike every other invention that has advanced humanity, Harari believes AI should not be considered a tool.

“If you look at fire, you can do many, many things with fire, but you make the decisions; it’s not the fire’s decision … AI is different because it can make decisions by itself and can invent new ideas by itself,” he said.

Harari noted that it is very hard to appreciate what it means when AI agents are not considered merely as tools. As they get smarter, he warned that they will be harder to control.

As an example, he said: “Just as chickens cannot understand mathematics, which is the basis of our financial system, I don’t know how many years away we are from an analogous situation when there is a new financial system based on a new mathematics which is just way beyond the capacity of the human brain.”
